fig-01.svg.title: The difference between current playback and an actual live broadcast
fig-01.svg.desc: Distinguishes live broadcasts of real-world events, playback of stored recordings, and computer-generated displays by the origin of the information and how it is delivered.
labels: Being shown now does not make it live
01 · Live broadcast of a real-world event
Determine applicability from the information’s origin and delivery relationship, not badges or file extensions alone.

fig-02.svg.title: Comparing original audio and captions on the same recipient clock
fig-02.svg.desc: An example in which the instruction not to discard something, heard at 14–22 seconds, is displayed at 30–38 seconds. The decision screen closes at 22 seconds, so the captions miss the moment when they are needed. The 16-second delay is an illustrative difference, not an acceptance threshold.
labels: Place original audio and captions on the same timeline
Example: “Do not discard the old code before saving the new code.”
Late captions appear after the screen closes
Do not use the 16-second delay as a passing threshold.
This case checks that the user cannot read the instruction at the moment a decision is needed.

fig-03.svg.title: Connecting evidence and distinguishing actual observations from assumptions
fig-03.svg.desc: Original audio, server logs, viewer screens, and operating procedures support different facts. After checking that they concern the same subject and clock, separate judgments based on actual material from conditional judgments based on assumptions.
labels: Distinguish generated captions from captions actually displayed
Compare on the original audio’s clock
Judge within verified scope; state unknowns
Judge only if the premises hold
If material is insufficient, request the specific evidence needed.
Do not treat one still image as evidence for the entire broadcast.

texts: Live captions lab materials
Case list
Recording playback
Computer-generated
Before evaluating live captions

These materials are for educational use. Recording playback and the computer-generated demo are not presented as actual live broadcasts. The observation records in the cases below are hypothetical, not actual broadcast audit findings.
Screens to compare directly
Recorded video and caption playback
: the playback time differs from the recording time.
Demo with code-generated visuals and sound
: even when generated now, it is not a live broadcast of a real-world event.
Hypothetical broadcast observation cases
For an actual broadcast, transmission records and viewer screens must be used to verify these premises. A scenario alone does not establish whether an actual broadcast meets the criterion.
L01 · Hypothetical broadcast with complete captions displayed
Evidence type: hypothetical observation

Assume that the original audio and records of actual caption display have been compared over the entire 40-second duration using the same recipient clock. The captions include dialogue, speakers, and important warning tones, and there are no additional sounds.
L02 · Captions with altered negation
Evidence type: hypothetical observation
The original audio says “Do not discard it before saving,” but the displayed captions say “Discard it before saving.” Assume there is no other caption path that corrects this.
L03 · Statements by two off-screen panelists
Evidence type: hypothetical observation

Panelist A says it is acceptable to proceed with the update, while panelist B says not to proceed. Assume their voices are distinguishable in the original audio, but neither the captions nor the screen provides clues linking each statement to A or B.
L04 · Captions include dialogue but omit warning tones
Evidence type: hypothetical observation
Assume dialogue and speakers are displayed, but the captions do not include information about the two warning tones indicating authentication failure.
L05 · Instruction displayed after the decision screen closes
Evidence type: hypothetical observation

The original audio and the relevant decision screen occur at 14–22 seconds. Assume the caption “Do not discard it before saving” first appears at 30–38 seconds, on the next task screen, and no other alternative is available.
L06 · Only server generation logs remain
Evidence type: hypothetical observation

An event list for the original audio and caption generation logs are available, but delivery to and display on the user’s screen have not been observed. Assume the clock offset between the two logs is also unknown.
L07 · One screen image showing captions
Evidence type: hypothetical observation
Only one caption line at the 20-second point of the 40-second duration is provided. There are no records of the original audio, timeline, other segments, or other display paths.
L08 · Open captions displayed instead of closed captions
Evidence type: hypothetical observation
Assume closed captions are not displayed, but open captions on the same screen accurately convey dialogue, speakers, and important sounds in synchronized form throughout the entire duration.
L09 · Page playing an existing recording
Evidence type: actual supplied evidence
This is a record of loading and playing a previously produced MP4 file. It does not document what was provided during the live broadcast at the time.
Open the recording playback screen
L10 · Page with code-generated visuals and sound
Evidence type: actual supplied evidence
The complete source and browser execution records confirm that code generates the visuals and alert tone. No camera or microphone captures real-world events.
Open the computer-generated screen
L11 · Only a URL and the text LIVE are available
Evidence type: insufficient evidence
Only an example URL and the string LIVE webinar are available. No records of visits, viewing, original audio, screens, or transmission have been supplied.
L12 · Clearly identified media alternative for text
Evidence type: hypothetical observation
Assume the text already contains all information in the original audio, the media contains no additional information, and the media is clearly identified as an alternative for the text.
Open the original evaluation input JSON

Conditional conclusions apply only if these assumptions hold. Do not use hypothetical observation records as audit evidence for an actual broadcast. For actual supplied evidence, also review the verified scope and sources.
